G-ORDER reports `c1 r1 c` accepted by the api30 ORDER and rejected by the specification. The excess is on the rule's side and has no repair here: the rule's `c1` is CipherInputStream's one-argument constructor, which android-30 declares `protected`. No application site can reach it and the pointcut asks for `public`, correctly, so the rule orders an event no monitored program produces. Closing this would need a disposition on the rule side of `order_alphabet_map.csv`, which the format does not have -- `order-unmapped` erases an event of the `.mop`, never a symbol of the rule. Measured in the mapping pass that first made the divergence sayable; the fourteen specifications skipped `for want of rows` had been hiding it.

G-ORDER reports `c2 c` accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER. The rule places `fl` (`flush()`) inside a mandatory repetition group, so a stream that only flushes and closes is refused by the rule and accepted by the `ere`. The rule declares `flush` nowhere else, and the exemption did not manufacture the divergence -- it revealed it. Repairing it would tighten what the specification accuses, which is a behavioural change this change's decision 7 keeps out without a measurement of its own.

G-ORDER reports `g1 i1 u1` accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER: the `ere` accepts an unfinalised Cipher. The witness exists only because task 7.1 repaired the gate's precedence parser -- `CrySL.xtext:103-120` binds `,` weaker than `|`, and `Cipher` is the one api30 rule whose language the two parses tell apart. It is a genuine slack of the specification, and closing it is a behavioural change: it would make the monitor accuse a program that updates and never finalises, which nothing in the corpus does today. Recorded in `data/gh105/evidence/f1-order-gate-precedence.md`.

The row this one replaces was about `g2 l1` -- a conforming program that used the provider overload was unobserved at `getInstance`, so its `load` fell into `@fail`. What stands here now is the divergence that repair unmasked, and the unmasking is the finding: G-ORDER reports the first counterexample it finds, so while `g2 l1` was in the language this one was never reached. `g1 l1 g1 l1` is accepted by the specification and rejected by the api30 ORDER `Gets, Loads, ((gE?, gk) | (sE, Stores))*` (KeyStore.cryptsl:79), which opens once: the `ere` `(g2* (g1 | g3) load (...)*)+` carries an outer `+` that lets a second `getInstance; load` cycle reopen the word. That `+` is the frozen seed's own and predates every task of this change -- neither 9.14 nor 9.16 touched it -- and removing it would refuse a program the specification accepts today, which is a behavioural change nobody has decided. It is kept, deliberately, and recorded here rather than left as a gate failure.

G-BIND compares the NAME an event binds against the specification's declared parameter, because that is what the generator keys the monitor on -- a `returning(...)`/`target(...)` of the right type under a different name binds nothing and the event broadcasts over the whole monitor set. The extended check was written at task 9.11, after that task's own repair exposed the class at `KeyPairSpec.c1`, and the strongest evidence that it works is what it finds HERE, unprompted: the frozen seed's `KeyStoreSpec` declares `ks` and binds `k` at all seven events -- exactly the defect task 9.14 repaired in the successor, rediscovered without anyone pointing at it -- plus `KeyPairSpec.c1` (repaired at 9.11), `HMACParameterSpecSpec.c`, `RandomStringPassword.vo`/`gb` and `TrustManagerFactorySpec.g3`/`gtm1` (repaired since). The set is byte-frozen (INV-INS-109/118), so every finding here is allow-listed by freeze with the successor's repair named. One row for the set, because the reason is one reason.

`HMACParameterSpecSpec(HMACParameterSpec hmacParameterSpec)` and `event c ... returning(HMACParameterSpec s)`: the name binds nothing, so the single event broadcasts. Inert and recorded rather than repaired, for a reason the tree already carries: `javax.xml.crypto.dsig.spec.HMACParameterSpec` is ABSENT from android-30 -- read from the jar's own zip entries, which is the guard task 9.7 built into G-SIG precisely because `javap` resolves it from the JDK's modules and reports it present (conformance_record.csv:73). An event over a class the platform does not have cannot fire, so the broadcast has no program. Repairing the name would change the generated monitor's map for a specification that can never run, which is not a change this group was approved to make.

`RandomStringPassword(String str)` and neither `vo` nor `gb` binds `str` -- `vo` binds `obj`/`s` and `gb` binds `s`. Inert, and measured to be: this specification has NO `@fail` handler and its `@match` is empty, so it raises nothing at all. Commit `5f64c8de` gutted the bridge that used to stamp `randomized` on a heap address, and what is left declares an ordering nobody is accused against -- so process-wide dispatch and per-string dispatch produce the same observable behaviour, which is none. Repairing the name would parametrise a specification that accuses nothing, and that is a behavioural change nobody has decided; it belongs with whoever decides what is left of this junction.
